1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 d6.name: Ruy Lopez: Steinitz Defence
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 d6.background: The favourite of the first world champion, Wilhelm Steinitz, and often played by Emanuel Lasker and José Raúl Capablanca. It largely fell into disuse after the First World War.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 d6 4.d4.strategy: Attacks e5 a second time and, with the c6 knight pinned, genuinely threatens to win the pawn. Black must trade pawns or break the pin, so White forces the issue at once and gets a lasting space advantage whichever way Black decides.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 d6 4.d4.name: Ruy Lopez: Steinitz Defence
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 d6 4.d4.background: Wilhelm Steinitz did not fully appreciate 4.d4, which is today understood to be the most critical continuation.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 d6 4.d4 Bd7.strategy: Breaks the pin and defends the pawn on e5 in one move: an exchange on c6 can now be answered by the bishop, so nothing is won on e5. Black keeps the stronghold, at the price of a cramped position in which the d6 pawn shuts in the dark-squared bishop.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 d6 4.d4 exd4.strategy: Trades pawns before White can win one, but gives up the stronghold on e5. White's knight recaptures into the centre and keeps a lasting space edge, so Black must defend a cramped but solid position.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 d6 4.d4 Bd7 5.Nc.strategy: Guards e4 and renews the threat to e5: after the exchange on c6 and the capture on e5 the e4 pawn can no longer be won back by the bishop, so a pawn is really at stake. White develops and keeps the initiative while Black stays cramped.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 d6 4.d4 Bd7 5.c4.name: Ruy Lopez: Steinitz Defence, Semi-Duras Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 d6 4.d4 Bd7 5.c4.strategy: Gains space on the queenside but, instead of guarding e4, leaves it undefended, so the threat against e5 is gone: Black can trade on d4 or attack e4 with a developing move. White settles for a space edge with a looser centre.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 d6 4.d4 Bd7 5.Nc.strategy: Develops with an attack on e4, so that capturing on e5 no longer wins a pawn: ...Bxe4 or ...Nxe4 regains it at once. Black completes development and holds the centre solidly.

Brings the king to safety and keeps all the pressure on e5 and the option of exchanging on c6. It is the sound way to continue development; Black must soon decide how to resolve the tension in the centre.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 d6 4.d4 Bd7 5.Nc.name: Ruy Lopez: Steinitz Defence, Nimzowitsch Attack
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 d6 4.d4 Bd7 5.Nc.strategy: Trades the bishop for the knight to remove a defender of e5, but Black recaptures with the bishop, so the pawn structure stays intact and e5 is not really attacked. White gives up the bishop pair for little in return.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 d6 4.d4 Bd7 5.Nc.name: Ruy Lopez: Berlin Defence, Hedgehog Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 d6 4.d4 Bd7 5.Nc.strategy: Develops the bishop and prepares to castle, but only once the centre is settled: with White's rook heading for e1, castling at once runs into a tactic that loses material, so Black will have to exchange on d4. Solid, but passive.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 d6 4.d4 Bd7 5.Nc.name: Ruy Lopez: Berlin Defence, Closed Wolf Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 d6 4.d4 Bd7 5.Nc.strategy: Resolves the centre at once, before White's rook reaches the e-file, and so avoids the tactics around castling. The price is the e5 stronghold: White's knight recaptures into the centre with a freer game, but Black's pieces are well placed and the structure is sound.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 d6 4.d4 exd4 5.O.name: Ruy Lopez: Steinitz Defence, Centre Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 d6 4.d4 exd4 5.O.strategy: Castles before recapturing on d4. The pinned c6 knight cannot take the pawn, and unpinning with ...Bd7 just lets White recapture. A harmless delay that gains nothing over the direct recapture and lets Black try to keep the pawn.
